{{Short description|Type of vector space in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Lagrangian Grassmannian''' is the [[smooth manifold]] of [[Lagrangian subspace]]s of a real [[symplectic vector space]] ''V''. Its dimension is {{sfrac|1|2}}''n''(''n'' + 1) (where the dimension of ''V'' is ''2n''). It may be identified with the [[homogeneous space]]

:{{Math|U(''n'')/O(''n'')}},

where {{Math|U(''n'')}} is the [[unitary group]] and {{Math|O(''n'')}} the [[orthogonal group]]. Following [[Vladimir Arnold]] it is denoted by Λ(''n''). The Lagrangian Grassmannian is a submanifold of the ordinary [[Grassmannian]] of '''V'''.

A ''' complex Lagrangian Grassmannian''' is the [[homogeneous space|complex homogeneous manifold]] of [[Lagrangian subspace]]s of a complex  [[symplectic vector space]] ''V'' of dimension 2''n''. It may be identified with the [[homogeneous space]] of complex dimension {{sfrac|1|2}}''n''(''n'' + 1)

:{{Math|Sp(''n'')/U(''n'')}},

where {{Math|Sp(''n'')}} is the [[symplectic group|compact symplectic group]].

==As a homogeneous space==

To see that the Lagrangian Grassmannian Λ(''n'') can be identified with {{Math|U(''n'')/O(''n'')}}, note that <math>\mathbb{C}^n</math> is a 2''n''-dimensional real vector space, with the imaginary part of its usual inner product making it into a symplectic vector space.  The Lagrangian subspaces of <math>\mathbb{C}^n</math> are then the real subspaces <math>L \subseteq \mathbb{C}^n</math> of real dimension ''n'' on which the imaginary part of the inner product vanishes.   An example is <math>\mathbb{R}^n \subseteq \mathbb{C}^n</math>.  The [[unitary group]] {{Math|U(''n'')}} acts transitively on the set of these subspaces, and the stabilizer of <math>\mathbb{R}^n</math> is the [[orthogonal group]] <math>\mathrm{O}(n) \subseteq \mathrm{U}(n)</math>.  It follows from the theory of [[Homogeneous_space#Homogeneous_spaces_as_coset_spaces|homogeneous spaces]] that Λ(''n'') is isomorphic to {{Math|U(''n'')/O(''n'')}} as a homogeneous space of {{Math|U(''n'')}}. 

It is a compact manifold of dimension <math>n(n+1)/2</math>. It is a (real, nonsingular) projective algebraic variety. Given a Lagrangian subspace A, the set of Lagranigian subspaces complementary to A is affine.  Given an arbitrary complementary subspace B, this affine space consists of the graphs of symmetric linear operators <math>u:B\to A</math>, <math>G(u) = \{b + u(b) | b\in B\}</math>. This is an affine space of dimension <math>n(n+1)/2</math> since the dimensions of A and B are both n. Symmetry here means that the form <math>\omega(b,u(b'))</math> is a symmetric form on B. Likewise, the tangent space at a lagrangian subspace A is the space of symmetric opeators <math>A\to A^*</math>.

From the fibration
<math display=block> 1\to O(n)\to U(n)\to \Lambda(n)</math>
the [[fundamental group]] may be inferred from the [[long exact homotopy sequence]]:
<math display=block>\pi_1(\Lambda(n)) = \mathbb Z.</math>

==Topology==
The stable topology of the Lagrangian Grassmannian and complex Lagrangian Grassmannian is completely understood, as these spaces appear in the [[Bott periodicity theorem]]: <math>\Omega(\mathrm{Sp}/\mathrm U) \simeq \mathrm U/\mathrm O</math>, and <math>\Omega(\mathrm U/ \mathrm O) \simeq \mathbb{Z}\times \mathrm{BO}</math> – they are thus exactly the [[Orthogonal group#Homotopy groups|homotopy groups of the stable orthogonal group]], up to a shift in indexing (dimension).

In particular, the [[fundamental group]] of <math>U/O</math> is [[infinite cyclic]]. Its first [[homology group]] is therefore also infinite cyclic, as is its first [[cohomology group]], with a distinguished generator given by the square of the [[determinant]] of a [[unitary matrix]], as a mapping to the [[unit circle]]. Arnold showed that this leads to a description of the '''Maslov index''', introduced by [[V. P. Maslov]].

For a [[Lagrangian submanifold]] ''M'' of ''V'', in fact, there is a mapping

:<math>M\to\Lambda(n)</math>

which classifies its [[tangent space]] at each point (cf. [[Gauss map]]). The Maslov index is the pullback via this mapping, in

:<math>H^1(M, \mathbb{Z})</math>

of the distinguished generator of

:<math>H^1(\Lambda(n), \mathbb{Z})</math>.

The Lagrangian Grassmannian is the [[Shilov boundary]] of the [[Siegel upper half space]].

==Maslov index==
{{main|Maslov index}}

Given a fixed Lagrangian subspace <math>L</math> in the Lagrangian Grassmannian <math>\Lambda</math>, the subset
<math display="block">M_L=\{V\in\Lambda \mid V\cap L\neq 0\}</math>
is the ''Maslov cycle'', a singular hypersurface in <math>\Lambda</math>.<ref name="Arnold1967">{{cite journal
 |last=Arnold
 |first=V. I.
 |author-link=Vladimir Arnold
 |title=On a characteristic class entering in conditions of quantization
 |journal=Functional Analysis and Its Applications
 |volume=1
 |issue=1
 |year=1967
 |pages=1–13
}}</ref> For a generic path of Lagrangian subspaces in <math>\Lambda</math> whose endpoints are transverse to <math>L</math>, the '''Maslov index''' is the signed intersection number of the path with <math>M_L</math>.<ref name="RobbinSalamon1993">{{cite journal
 |last1=Robbin
 |first1=Joel
 |last2=Salamon
 |first2=Dietmar
 |title=The Maslov index for paths
 |journal=Topology
 |volume=32
 |issue=4
 |year=1993
 |pages=827–844
 |doi=10.1016/0040-9383(93)90052-W
}}</ref>  The Maslov index is invariant under homotopies of paths through Lagrangian subspaces, provided the endpoints remain transverse to the chosen reference Lagrangian <math>L</math>. For a loop, it depends only on the homotopy class of the loop and is independent of the choice of <math>L</math>.<ref name="Arnold1967" /><ref name="RobbinSalamon1993" />

The Maslov index is important in the study of [[Caustic_(optics)|caustics]] and semiclassical asymptotics. Roughly speaking, when a family of Lagrangian subspaces crosses the Maslov cycle, one encounters a caustic relative to the chosen reference Lagrangian <math>L</math>; in the theory of [[Fourier integral operator]]s and the [[WKB approximation]], such crossings produce phase corrections governed by the Maslov index.<ref name="Hormander1971">{{cite journal
 |last=Hörmander
 |first=Lars |author-link=Lars Hörmander
 |title=Fourier integral operators. I
 |journal=Acta Mathematica
 |volume=127
 |year=1971
 |pages=79–183
 |doi=10.1007/BF02392052
}}</ref><ref name="Duistermaat1996">{{cite book
 |last=Duistermaat
 |first=J. J.
 |title=Fourier Integral Operators
 |series=Progress in Mathematics
 |volume=130
 |publisher=Birkhäuser
 |location=Boston
 |year=1996
 |isbn=978-0-8176-8107-4
}}</ref>
